input_signals.name: Gross-Profit Repurchaser Versus Issuer
input_signals.hypothesis: Identical operating strength maps to opposite expected returns depending on the direction of equity flow: high gross profitability at a net repurchaser signals underpriced cash generation, while the same profitability at a net equity issuer signals a management team monetizing a rich valuation.
input_signals.reasoning: Substituting the bounded, non-negative industry rank of gross profitability for the signed z-score fixes the internal inconsistency the critic identified: a negative profitability score can no longer be flipped positive by the issuer sign, so distressed issuers now sit near zero in the middle rather than at the top. The resulting ordering is exactly the stated economics — profitable repurchasers at the top, profitable issuers at the bottom, weak firms of either financing type in the middle — a genuinely non-monotone conditioning of the profitability premium on financing direction.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), sign( sub( prstkc, sstk ) ) )

input_signals.name: Peak-Profit Equity Issuance
input_signals.hypothesis: Issuance timed to a firm's own profitability peak is the sharpest market-timing tell, because that is when reported fundamentals most flatter the equity price; conversely, buying back stock at a self-referenced profit peak signals management believes the shares are cheap even against strong current numbers.
input_signals.reasoning: The conditioner is the firm's position in its *own* five-year profitability distribution rather than the cross-sectional profitability level, so the signal no longer fights the documented profitability premium and is not a relabeling of net share issuance. Because TS_RANK is bounded in [0,1] and the financing leg is signed, the short leg is peak-profit issuers and the long leg is peak-profit repurchasers, while trough-profitability firms — whose issuance is need-driven, not opportunistic — are compressed toward zero.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ts_rank( ratio( oiadp, at ), 5 ), ratio( sub( sstk, prstkc ), at ) )

input_signals.name: Cash Yield On Lifetime Capital Supplied
input_signals.hypothesis: The economically relevant quantity is how much internal cash a firm has produced per dollar of capital outsiders have actually had to supply; firms that generate large cumulative operating cash flow on a small externally funded base are efficient compounders, while capital-hungry firms with thin cash generation are chronically dependent and overvalued.
input_signals.reasoning: This is a genuine ratio interaction rather than the rank difference the critic called an accounting identity: external raises enter the denominator as invested capital, so a heavy issuer that converts the money into cash flow is not penalized, which is precisely what separates it from composite issuance. Anchoring the denominator with current assets keeps it strictly positive and well-behaved for non-issuers, and the five-year window measures cycle-length funding efficiency rather than a single year's flow.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ratio( ts_sum( oancf, 5 ), add( at, ts_sum( add( sstk, dltis ), 5 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Internally Funded Capital Return
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3)), WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), at), RATIO(SUB(dltis, dltr), at)), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: What matters is not whether a profitable firm returns capital but where the cash comes from: distributions funded out of operations reveal genuine surplus, while distributions financed by simultaneous net borrowing are balance-sheet engineering that raises future refinancing risk without creating value.
input_signals.reasoning: Gen-0 payout signals treated all distributions alike; subtracting net debt issuance from net equity payout separates the "borrowed buyback" firms from true cash generators, a funding-source channel none of the archive signals test. Conditioning on a persistent cash-based profitability rank keeps the interaction genuine — the signed leg only carries weight for firms with a credible operating cash base — and winsorization guards against the tail problem that killed the gen-0 alphas.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ma( ratio( oancf, at ), 3 ) ), winsor( sub( ratio( sub( add( prstkc, dvc ), sstk ), at ), ratio( sub( dltis, dltr ), at ) ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: Volatile-Earnings Leverage Build
input_signals.hypothesis: Debt expansion is only informative in interaction with the reliability of the cash flows meant to service it: firms with unstable operating profitability that lever up are taking on default risk the market underweights, while equally unstable firms retiring debt are de-risking, and firms with steady profits can absorb leverage changes with little return consequence.
input_signals.reasoning: This introduces a second-moment profitability channel absent from the entire archive, which so far conditions only on the level, trend, or cash-conversion of profits. The volatility rank acts as a bounded amplifier so stable earners are compressed toward zero, making the sort a clean contrast between fragile levering firms and fragile deleveraging firms rather than a restatement of the known debt-issuance anomaly.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( vol( ratio( oiadp, at ), 5 ) ), winsor( growth( add( dltt, dlc ), 1 ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: Rollover Exposure Meets Cash Cover
input_signals.hypothesis: The maturity structure of a firm's debt only matters in interaction with its ability to self-fund: heavy reliance on short-term debt is benign for a firm generating ample operating cash but is a repricing risk for a cash-thin firm that must refinance into uncertain credit conditions, so cash cover is compensated precisely where rollover exposure is greatest.
input_signals.reasoning: This introduces a debt-maturity channel that no archive signal touches — prior work here used only the level, change, or direction of total financing flows, never its composition — and it is measured from balance-sheet items available for nearly all firms, so coverage should be well above the 0.08–0.13 range that weakened earlier tests. The short-term-debt share is a bounded weight in [0,1] and the industry z-score of cash-based profitability is signed and smoothly distributed, so both tails are populated by high-rollover firms differing in cash cover rather than by lumpy zero-inflated flows.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( dlc, add( dltt, dlc ) ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( oancf, at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Habitual Financing Direction Under Profit
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(oiadp, at), 3)), SUB(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(SUB(sstk, prstkc), 0), 5), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(SUB(prstkc, sstk), 0), 5)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A single year of issuance is noisy timing, but a five-year habit reveals financing policy: a persistently profitable firm that is a net issuer year after year is chronically dependent on outside equity despite reported strength, while a persistently profitable serial repurchaser is credibly converting operating strength into shareholder cash.
input_signals.reasoning: The critic is right that 1% winsorization cannot change rank-based decile sorts, so the correct diagnosis of the earlier FMB-without-alpha result is zero inflation and lumpy magnitudes, not tail outliers; replacing the continuous issuance-to-assets magnitude with a bounded net count of issuing minus repurchasing years in [-5, +5] removes scale entirely and populates the whole support with economically comparable firms. It also changes the economic content from a one-year timing event to a persistent financing policy interacted with sustained operating profitability, so it tests habit rather than opportunism.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ma( ratio( oiadp, at ), 3 ) ), sub( ts_sum( indicator( sub( sstk, prstkc ), 0 ), 5 ), ts_sum( indicator( sub( prstkc, sstk ), 0 ), 5 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Cost Of Debt Conditioned Profitability
input_signals.hypothesis: The interest rate a firm actually pays is the credit market's revealed assessment of its risk, and equity investors underreact to the conflict when that assessment disagrees with operating performance: a firm paying a high price for debt while generating strong operating income is being over-penalized, whereas expensive debt plus weak operating income confirms genuine distress.
input_signals.reasoning: No archive signal uses the *price* of external financing — only its quantity, direction, or maturity — so this introduces the credit-market-versus-equity-market disagreement channel. Realized cost of debt is a bounded, slow-moving state variable available for all levered firms, and pairing it with a smooth operating-margin z-score keeps the tails populated by economically comparable high-yield borrowers that differ in operating strength.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( xint, add( dltt, dlc ) ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( oibdp, at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Dividend Commitment Meets Cash Cover
input_signals.hypothesis: Dividends are a quasi-fixed obligation, so what matters is the cash cushion remaining after the commitment is honored: a heavy dividend payer that still retains ample operating cash is signaling durable surplus, while a heavy payer whose operating cash barely covers or fails to cover the dividend faces a cut the market has not discounted.
input_signals.reasoning: This applies the winning obligation-conditioning architecture to the payout side rather than the debt side, testing whether the rollover result reflects fixed obligations generally or debt specifically — an economically informative contrast rather than a formula variant. Dividend intensity is a bounded, extremely persistent state and post-dividend cash flow is smooth and two-sided, so the short leg is the economically meaningful set of stretched payers rather than a handful of extreme-flow observations.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( dvt, at ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( oancf, dvt ), at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Net Share Retirement Tilt Under Profit
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(ib, at), 3)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), ADD(dvt, prstkc)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Gross repurchases overstate insider conviction for firms that simultaneously issue stock to employees or acquirers, so the price-signalling content of the distribution mix should be concentrated in the fraction of distributions that constitutes genuine net share retirement rather than recycled equity.
input_signals.reasoning: This isolates a single design choice against Signal 1 — netting issuance out of the repurchase leg — which directly tests whether the instrument-choice alpha comes from real shrinkage of the equity base or merely from the accounting label on the distribution. It matters economically because option-heavy firms buy back large amounts while their share count still grows, and if the effect survives the netting we learn the channel is genuine capital return rather than a dividend-payer style exposure.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ma( ratio( ib, at ), 3 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( prstkc, sstk ), add( dvt, prstkc ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Repurchase Tilt Meets Free Cash Cover
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dvt), at), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(prstkc, ADD(dvt, prstkc)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A repurchase-tilted distribution policy is only a credible valuation signal when the firm still holds surplus cash after honoring its dividend commitment; buybacks executed by cash-strapped firms are cosmetic EPS management rather than an informed purchase of undervalued equity.
input_signals.reasoning: This fuses the archive's two strongest results — the instrument-mix effect and post-dividend cash cover (alpha +2.7%, t = 2.28) — by replacing the accrual profitability weight with the cash-cover weight, testing whether the mix signal is amplified precisely where the cash to execute exists. Because both winners load on different data (accrual earnings versus operating cash net of committed payout), a strengthening here would indicate the two effects are complementary rather than the same exposure measured twice.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( sub( oancf, dvt ), at ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( prstkc, add( dvt, prstkc ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Dividend Rigidity Meets Cash Generation
input_signals.hypothesis: The severity of a dividend commitment is best measured against normalized operating income, and the cash cushion backing it is best measured independently of that commitment: firms pledging a large share of normal earnings to dividends are safe only if their operating cash generation is strong, and are cut candidates otherwise.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive's second-best signal put dvt in both the weight and the signed leg, so weight and signal were mechanically negatively related and the critic correctly warned the result may reduce to post-dividend cash flow among payers; here the rigidity weight uses smoothed operating income and the signed leg uses unadjusted operating cash flow, eliminating the shared term. If the alpha survives this decoupling the commitment-versus-cover mechanism is real, and coverage should rise from 0.091 toward the 0.13 seen for the payout-ratio-weighted construction.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( dvt, ma( oibdp, 3 ) ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( oancf, at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Internally Funded Innovation
input_signals.hypothesis: R&D-intensive firms differ sharply in who pays for the innovation: those funding research from internal cash while retiring shares have proven the research is self-sustaining, whereas those funding it by repeatedly tapping equity markets are dependent on investor sentiment and are systematically overvalued at the moment of issuance.
input_signals.reasoning: This introduces the innovation-funding channel, which no archive signal touches, and it interacts a real-investment characteristic with financing direction rather than re-slicing distribution policy for a fifth time. Treating unreported R&D as zero is the economically correct convention rather than a coverage patch, so the weight is defined for all firms and collapses non-innovators toward zero, leaving the spread to contrast research-heavy self-funders against research-heavy serial issuers.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( coalesce( ratio( xrd, at ), 0 ) ), neg( ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( sstk, prstkc ), at ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Adjustment Versus Postponement
input_signals.hypothesis: When operating profitability deteriorates a firm must either adjust — shrinking its balance sheet and retiring debt — or postpone by borrowing to bridge the shortfall; the postponers accumulate leverage against a weakening cash base and are repriced later, while the adjusters have already taken the pain.
input_signals.reasoning: This abandons the own-cycle issuance interaction the critic showed was a sign-flipped restatement and instead conditions on a *deterioration event*, asking what the firm does about it — a managerial-response channel that no archive signal tests and that is distinct from both the volatility-conditioned and the improvement-conditioned leverage signals already evaluated. The bounded rank of profitability decline concentrates the signal in firms actually facing the choice, while the signed debt-growth z-score keeps both the levering and deleveraging responses in the tails rather than discarding one side.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( neg( winsor( delta( ratio( oiadp, at ), 1 ), 1 ) ) ), neg( ind_zscore( winsor( growth( add( dltt, dlc ), 1 ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Dividend Funded By Shareholders
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm that pays dividends and issues equity in the same year is handing cash to one set of shareholders while collecting it from another, and whether this round trip is benign or pathological depends entirely on internal cash: with strong operating cash flow it reflects options and acquisition currency, but with weak cash flow the dividend is literally being financed by shareholders and cannot last.
input_signals.reasoning: The MIN of dividends and equity issuance measures the *simultaneity* of the two flows, a quantity no difference or ratio of the same variables can express and one that no archive signal has used, so this is not another slice of net payout or composite issuance. It applies the conditioning architecture that has produced this archive's alphas — a bounded, mostly-zero weight that isolates the affected population, scaling a smooth two-sided cash-profitability z-score — and the short tail is the economically sharp set of cash-poor firms recycling shareholder money into dividends.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( min( dvt, sstk ), at ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( oancf, at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Innovation Funding Source Neutralized
input_signals.hypothesis: Research-intensive firms that finance innovation from internal cash while retiring shares have demonstrated the research is self-sustaining, whereas research-intensive firms repeatedly tapping equity markets depend on sentiment and are systematically overvalued when they issue; firms doing no research carry no information in this channel at all.
input_signals.reasoning: The critic correctly identified that COALESCE-to-zero R&D still gives every non-innovator a large tied IND_RANK weight, so most of the fmb 5.12 spread was the plain net issuance anomaly; using the raw winsorized R&D-to-sales intensity as the weight sets non-innovators to exactly zero, which places them in the middle of the sort and leaves both tails populated only by genuine innovators. This is a construction fix that makes the strongest cross-sectional slope in the archive interpretable and should raise the FF5 alpha above its diluted 1.9%.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( coalesce( ratio( xrd, sale ), 0 ), 1 ), neg( ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( sstk, prstkc ), at ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Distribution Commitment Against Cash Floor
input_signals.hypothesis: What protects a distribution policy is not average profitability but the worst year the firm has had: committed distributors whose five-year minimum operating cash flow is still comfortably positive can maintain the policy through a downturn, while those whose floor is near or below zero are one bad year from a cut.
input_signals.reasoning: Every profitability leg tested so far uses a level, change, trend, or volatility, but never the downside floor, and a minimum is economically the right statistic when the question is whether a fixed commitment survives — it is also distinct from volatility, which the archive already showed is uninformative on the financing side. The commitment weight is bounded and the floor z-score is smooth and two-sided, matching the architecture that has produced every reliable alpha here.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( add( dvt, prstkc ), at ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( ts_min( ratio( oancf, at ), 5 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Equity Recycled Against Distributions
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(MIN(sstk, ADD(dvt, prstkc)), at), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(oancf, at), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm handing cash to shareholders through dividends or buybacks while simultaneously selling stock is recycling equity rather than returning it, and whether that recycling is benign depends on internal cash: cash-rich recyclers are managing option dilution and currency for deals, while cash-poor recyclers are funding distributions with new investors' money.
input_signals.reasoning: The critic's binding argument is decisive and is fixed by construction here: because equity sales are almost always smaller than total distributions for established distributors, the MIN binds on the issuance side, so the weight measures recycled equity rather than degenerating into payout intensity. Relative to the archive's best-Sharpe signal this changes exactly one thing — extending the distribution side from dividends alone to dividends plus repurchases — which tests whether the recycling mechanism also captures option-heavy buyback firms whose share count still grows.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( min( sstk, add( dvt, prstkc ) ), at ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( oancf, at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Recycling Against Post Distribution Cash
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(MIN(sstk, ADD(dvt, prstkc)), at), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(oancf, ADD(dvt, prstkc)), at), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Recycling equity is pathological exactly when the firm's operations cannot cover what it hands out: a recycler whose operating cash exceeds its total distributions is managing dilution from a position of surplus, while a recycler whose distributions exceed operating cash is literally passing new shareholders' money through to old ones.
input_signals.reasoning: The winning signal used gross operating cash flow, which measures capacity in the abstract; netting out the distributions the firm actually committed to makes the signed leg the precise economic quantity the hypothesis names, and it is not collinear with the gross measure because distribution intensity varies enormously among recyclers. This changes one leg only, so the comparison against the 3.8% alpha benchmark is interpretable as a test of the coverage concept rather than of a new mechanism.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( min( sstk, add( dvt, prstkc ) ), at ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( oancf, add( dvt, prstkc ) ), at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Buyback Issuance Treadmill
input_signals.hypothesis: The purest form of capital recycling is a firm repurchasing and issuing stock at the same time, which returns no capital at all and merely offsets employee dilution; whether this treadmill is affordable depends entirely on operating cash, and cash-poor treadmill firms are spending scarce resources to mask compensation costs.
input_signals.reasoning: This decomposes the winning overlap by removing dividends from the distribution side, isolating the buyback-versus-issuance treadmill that the archive's mix and net-retirement signals both implicated but never measured directly. It answers a specific question left open by the parent signal — whether the effect is driven by dividend round trips or by option-offsetting repurchases — and the two populations barely intersect, so the result carries independent information.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( min( sstk, prstkc ), at ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( oancf, at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Persistent Equity Recycling
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm that distributes cash while issuing equity in every one of three consecutive years has institutionalized capital recycling rather than experienced a one-off deal or option-exercise year, and for these structural recyclers the adequacy of operating cash is a permanent characteristic that the market prices with a lag.
input_signals.reasoning: The critic is right that a three-year sum can be produced by one lumpy year, so the persistence screen is now implemented with TS_MIN, which is strictly positive only when the overlap occurred in all three years and whose magnitude is the smallest annual recycling amount. This makes the weight a true habit measure and should reduce the decile turnover and lumpiness that repeatedly separated strong slopes from tradable alpha elsewhere in this archive.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ts_min( ratio( min( sstk, add( dvt, prstkc ) ), at ), 3 ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( oancf, at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Recycling Without Share Shrinkage
input_signals.hypothesis: Recycling equity is only harmful if it fails to shrink the ownership base: a firm distributing and issuing on a scale large relative to its normal operating income but still reducing its share count has genuinely returned capital, while one whose share count keeps expanding has spent cash purely to absorb dilution and delivered nothing to continuing holders.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the ablation the critic objected to with a genuine candidate that closes the recycling story at its economic endpoint — the realized change in ownership — rather than at the cash flows, and the signed leg is the outcome variable rather than another profitability measure. Scaling the recycling weight by three-year normalized operating income makes the contradiction size-comparable across firms and supplies the profitability content, while the share-count leg is broadly reported so coverage should exceed the parent signal's 0.083.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( min( sstk, add( dvt, prstkc ) ), ma( oibdp, 3 ) ), 1 ) ), neg( ind_zscore( winsor( growth( csho, 1 ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Dilution Intensity Meets Cash Cover
input_signals.hypothesis: An expanding share base marks a firm that is absorbing outside equity in some form — offerings, acquisition currency, or compensation — and among such firms operating cash generation separates those diluting from strength against those diluting out of necessity.
input_signals.reasoning: Every strong signal in this family is capped at coverage 0.083 because it needs cash-flow-statement issuance data, whereas share count is reported by nearly all firms, so this tests whether the vulnerable population can be identified from the balance sheet at roughly 50% higher coverage. Critically it puts dilution on the *weight* side and keeps cash profitability on the signed side, the opposite of Recycling Without Share Shrinkage whose share-growth signed leg produced a strong slope with negative alpha — a direct test of my diagnosis that the leg, not the variable, was the problem.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( growth( csho, 1 ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( oancf, at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Recycling Meets Debt Service Slack
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(MIN(sstk, ADD(dvt, prstkc)), at), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(oibdp, xint), ADD(dltt, dlc)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Recycling equity is a choice for firms with financing slack and a necessity for firms without it: a recycler whose operating income after interest is large relative to its debt stock has untapped borrowing capacity and is managing dilution by preference, while one with thin coverage is issuing equity because credit markets are closed to it.
input_signals.reasoning: Every leg tested so far measures cash abundance relative to assets, whereas this measures capacity relative to existing claims, a genuinely different profitability dimension that remains a level concept — the only leg type that has ever produced alpha here. Debt-free recyclers land at the winsorized top, which is economically correct since they face no refinancing constraint at all, and the contrast against Signal 2 tells us whether the mechanism is about cash on hand or about access to alternative financing.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( min( sstk, add( dvt, prstkc ) ), at ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( oibdp, xint ), add( dltt, dlc ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Debt Funded Buybacks Meet Cash Cover
input_signals.hypothesis: Borrowing and repurchasing stock in the same year is a leverage-increasing recapitalization whose wisdom depends on cash generation: a cash-rich firm swapping cheap debt for expensive equity is exploiting a real cost-of-capital gap, while a cash-poor firm doing the same is manufacturing earnings per share with borrowed money and has consumed its remaining financing slack.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive has established that the signed leg must be a cash-generation level but that the conditioning *population* can be varied freely, and this identifies an entirely different population from the equity-recycling family — leverage-increasing recapitalizers rather than equity round-trippers — which no evaluated signal has isolated. The MIN binds on whichever leg is smaller so the weight measures the genuinely matched portion of the swap, and both inputs are common enough that coverage should match the 0.083 of the recycling line.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( min( dltis, prstkc ), at ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( oancf, at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Equity For Debt Substitution
input_signals.hypothesis: Selling stock and retiring debt in the same year is the mirror-image recapitalization and is usually creditor-driven: a firm with strong operating cash that deleverages through an equity raise is choosing a permanent capital base, whereas a cash-thin firm doing so is being forced by lenders to convert their claim into someone else's equity at whatever price the market will bear.
input_signals.reasoning: This is the economically opposite population to Signal 1 and to the entire distribution-based family — capital is flowing in from shareholders and out to creditors — so evaluating the two together maps which direction of recapitalization carries the mispricing rather than re-testing one mechanism twice. Debt retirement and equity sales are both directly reported flows, so the overlap is measured without inference and the weight is zero for the large majority of firms that do only one or neither.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( min( sstk, dltr ), at ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( oancf, at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Dual Market Dependence
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm drawing simultaneously on both the equity and debt markets in one year has exhausted internal funding and is maximally exposed to external capital conditions; among such firms, those still generating strong operating cash are financing genuine expansion while those generating little are funding a shortfall and will return to the market on worse terms.
input_signals.reasoning: This completes the map of simultaneity pairs with the case where both flows point inward, a population defined by dependence rather than by contradiction, and it is not reachable from any archived weight because net-financing constructions net the two sources against distributions instead of requiring both to be present. It also provides the cleanest discriminating test in the batch: if capital *inflow* simultaneity works as well as the distribution-versus-issuance contradiction, the mechanism is external dependence generally rather than the round trip specifically.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( min( sstk, dltis ), at ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( oancf, at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Cash Return On Shareholder Supplied Capital
input_signals.hypothesis: The right denominator for judging a firm's cash generation is the capital shareholders have actually committed, including money handed over in recent equity sales; firms producing large cumulative operating cash against a modest and slowly growing shareholder base are underpriced compounders, while serial issuers must keep enlarging that base to produce the same cash.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces a rank-weighted conditional with a functional form the archive has barely used since generation zero, where the analogous ratio produced a 1.8% alpha, but it changes the economics by measuring return on *shareholder-supplied* capital rather than on total capital, so serial equity issuers are penalized precisely in proportion to what they raised. The denominator is strictly positive for the vast majority of firms and requires only book equity plus issuance history, so it avoids the matched-flow missingness that caps the conditional family near 0.084 coverage.
input_signals.author: proposer

input_signals.name: Cash Rich Firms That Shrink Their Share Base
input_signals.hypothesis: This is the task's original economic story stated directly: among firms that generate real cash, those shrinking their ownership base are returning underpriced cash generation to holders, while those expanding it are either overvalued or covering a funding need that the reported cash flow conceals.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive's leader places dilution on the weight and cash on the signed leg; swapping the roles asks which side of the interaction actually carries the return information, and prior signed-financing legs failed only when the weight was an unstable income-scaled overlap, so the clean cash-profitability rank weight gives the construction a fair test. Together with Signal 1 this pins down the architecture question — main effect, interaction, or financing effect — that determines what the final generation should refine.

input_signals.name: Equity Absorption Meets Cash Earnings
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(ADD(SUB(GROWTH(ceq, 1), RATIO(ib, LAG(ceq, 1))), RATIO(dvt, LAG(ceq, 1))), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(ib, dp), at), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Book equity growing faster than retained earnings measures the dollars of capital shareholders actually handed over, which is a different and economically weightier quantity than the percentage change in share count — a large placement to one investor dilutes value without moving the count much, and vice versa for many small option exercises.
input_signals.reasoning: Share count and dollar absorption are distinct proxies for the same conditioning state, and the dollar version has never been evaluated here — the earlier attempt failed theme validation and its successor was flagged before testing — yet it is arguably the better measure of how much outside capital the firm consumed. Adding dividends back to the clean-surplus wedge isolates net issuance rather than issuance-less-payout, and all three inputs are broadly reported, so this rounds out the final set with the dollar-metric version of the winning population at full coverage.

input_signals.name: Dilution Meets Gross Profitability
input_signals.hypothesis: What justifies dilution is the underlying earning power of the business the new capital is buying into: a firm expanding its share base while producing wide gross profits per dollar of assets is scaling a genuinely productive operation, whereas one diluting on thin production economics is funding a business that does not yet work.
input_signals.reasoning: The critic is right that funds from operations is a collinear stand-in for operating cash flow, so this instead swaps in a profitability channel that is economically and statistically distinct — gross profit is measured above the cost line, is unaffected by working-capital timing, accrual policy, and depreciation choices, and is the cleanest available measure of business quality rather than cash timing. It also resolves the coverage constraint on its own terms, since revenue and cost of goods are reported for essentially the whole sample, and if the conditioning result survives a leg this different the mechanism is about firm quality interacting with financing rather than about cash-based profitability in disguise.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( growth( csho, 1 ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Conjunctive Cash Strength And Share Retirement
input_signals.hypothesis: The economic story of this task is conjunctive rather than multiplicative — the underpriced firm must be both genuinely cash-generative and actually returning capital, and failing either condition should disqualify it regardless of how extreme the other is.
input_signals.reasoning: Every signal in this archive aggregates its two themes by multiplication, which lets an extreme value on one leg carry a firm into the tail on its own; MIN of two bounded ranks is a genuinely different aggregator, never used here, and it enforces the joint condition the task describes so the long decile contains only firms strong on both dimensions. It replaces a deduction the critic showed was negligible with a structural change, it uses only broadly reported inputs, and it provides the final round's cleanest test of whether the conjunction outperforms the product.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( add( ib, dp ), at ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( neg( winsor( growth( csho, 1 ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Payout Commitment Meets Production Economics
input_signals.hypothesis: A rigid dividend is underwritten by the durability of the firm's unit economics, not by one year's cash conversion: a heavy payer whose products earn a wide gross spread can sustain the commitment through a downturn, while one with thin production margins is pledging cash it may not be able to earn.
input_signals.reasoning: Rather than substituting a near-identical cash proxy into an archived expression, this changes the economic content of the signed leg from cash timing to production profitability, which is the variable that determines whether a payout commitment is structurally supportable and which is close to orthogonal to cash conversion in the cross-section. It preserves the commitment family as a diversifier against the activity family in the final set while making the underwriting logic explicit, and gross profit's near-universal reporting lifts coverage above the 0.091 that has limited this line.
